newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico pension funds woo sceptical public.
newsitem.headline: Mexico pension funds woo sceptical public.

text.p: Seventeen firms are fighting for a slice of Mexico's landmark private pension system, but despite an Olympian advertising blitz, they are having trouble winning round a sceptical public, officials say.

On television and radio, on streets and in theatres, the Afores, as the private pension funds are known in Spanish, have hammered home a common message: savings under the new scheme will deliver a brighter future.

Expensive armies of sales staff have fanned out across the country to convince Mexicans to sign up with individual Afores, spelling out the benefits of a complex system that the government insists will make them wealthier than the old, practically bankrupt, pay-as-you go state scheme.

But the launch, begun on Feb. 3 and rounded off in late February with the approval of the final five of 17 Afores, has been far from smooth. Accused of charging hefty commissions and using underhand tactics to woo workers, the private funds have come under fire from unions, politicians and businessmen.

They have also faced a withering assault in the press that experts say may mean Mexico will have more trouble garnering support for private pension schemes than in other countries in Latin America where the experiment has been tested.

"I am very concerned about the negative publicity," said Camilo Salazar, vice president of Des Moines, Iowa-based Principal International Inc., whose Confia-Principal pension fund with Mexican partner Abaco was approved in late February.
"Why have industry and the government not responded? There was a lot less negative campaigning in Argentina and Chile," Salazar said.

In late February, the National Retirement Savings System Commission (Consar), the government watchdog, gave the green light to the government's only pension firm, known as Afore XXI, unleashing the full force of its fight to compete against 16 private competitors.

Afore XXI got a jump start from Mexican labour baron 96-year-old Fidel Velazquez, who with characteristic bluntness demanded that all 6 million members of his Confederation of Mexican Workers join it. He dubbed its rivals "speculators."
With a limit of 1.68 million workers in any one pension fund, there was no way that Velazquez's call could be heeded. But it annoyed the private funds nevertheless.
"It's absurd when he says 'Everyone affiliate, if you don't it's treason'," Manuel Reynaud, head of the newly-formed Mexican Afore Association, said.
"The duty of any union leader is to ensure that members have the most information possible and can choose freely," Reynaud said.
One of the arguments used by union leaders to discredit the private funds is the myriad foreign banks and insurance firms that have taken minority stakes in them.
That point may not wear well for long. Daniel Lederman, vice president of planning at Consar, said Bankers Trust New York Corp. is rumoured to be about to take a stake in the government's Afore XXI.
In another sign of discontent, critics have slammed the commissions announced by the Afores, in some cases as high as 25 percent of a worker's contribution.

One prominent business group in Monterrey said the high commissions would pay off in a single year some $600 million that the Afores had promised in start-up capital. But Lederman disputed the point, saying it would take up to eight years for the firms to become profitable.
He also noted that some Afores were dropping their commissions. Afore XXI, when it issued its own commissions, set them no lower than many of its private rivals.

Other missteps marked the first weeks of a system that the government hopes will revolutionise savings, but which officials acknowledge is stymied by a scepticism about Mexican finances in the aftermath of the peso crisis.

Lederman said one Afore, Bancrecer-Dresdner, could face sanctions because of a commercial -- which it quickly took off the air -- saying it would not charge commissions. In fact, it later explained, it would charge only on the balance of accounts, not on workers' contributions.

Pension executives say there are widespread suspicions that bribery is being contemplated to win large blocks of workers. They say union leaders have been doing the rounds asking for "incentives" -- which are illegal -- if they persuade their workers to join a particular Afore.
"Some union leaders seek money. They arrive and ask, "What do you offer?'," said Isaac Sacal, a sales manager at Afore Santander. He said his fund has never responded to such requests.
